prompt: Which order shows the increasing reactivity of alcohols toward HX?

choices.why: That is reversed. The HX method works best with tertiary alcohols, R3COH.
Methyl alcohol, CH3OH, is the least reactive of the four, below primary alcohols.

choices.text: All four classes react at about the same rate
choices.why: Tertiary alcohols react so fast that the reaction is run in cold ether; primary and secondary alcohols react much more slowly and need higher temperatures.

explanation: Treating an alcohol with HCl, HBr or HI is the simplest method, and it works best with tertiary alcohols, R3COH. Primary and secondary alcohols react much more slowly and at higher temperatures. The reactivity order is methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary.

prompt: How is the reaction of HX with a tertiary alcohol often carried out?

choices.text: By bubbling HCl or HBr gas into a cold ether solution of the alcohol
By heating the alcohol with HX at high temperature for a long time
choices.why: Slow, hot conditions are what primary and secondary alcohols need. Tertiary alcohols react so rapidly that cold conditions are enough.

choices.text: By treating the alcohol with SOCl2 or PBr3 instead
choices.why: SOCl2 and PBr3 are the reagents of choice for primary and secondary alcohols. Tertiary alcohols react readily with HX itself.

choices.text: By treating the alcohol with HF in pyridine
choices.why: HF in pyridine makes alkyl fluorides. Tertiary chlorides and bromides are made with HCl or HBr gas.

explanation: The reaction of HX with a tertiary alcohol is so rapid that it's often carried out simply by bubbling pure HCl or HBr gas into a cold ether solution of the alcohol. 1-Methylcyclohexanol, for example, gives 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane (90%) with HCl in ether at 0 °C.

prompt: What forms when HCl gas is bubbled into a cold ether solution of 1-methylcyclohexanol?

choices.why: Cl replaces the OH on the same carbon, carbon 1, which also carries the methyl group.
The methyl group stays; only the OH group is replaced by Cl.

choices.text: No product, because tertiary alcohols react too slowly with HX
choices.why: Tertiary alcohols are the most reactive toward HX; this reaction gives a 90% yield at 0 °C.

explanation: HCl converts the tertiary alcohol 1-methylcyclohexanol into 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane (90%), replacing the OH group by Cl and forming water.

prompt: Which reagents are best for converting primary and secondary alcohols into alkyl halides?

choices.text: HCl or HBr gas bubbled into cold ether
choices.why: That works well for tertiary alcohols. Primary and secondary alcohols react much more slowly with HX and need higher temperatures.
NBS replaces an allylic hydrogen with bromine (Section 10.3); it doesn't convert alcohols into alkyl halides.

choices.text: Chlorine (Cl2) or bromine (Br2) with ultraviolet light
choices.why: Radical halogenation replaces hydrogens of alkanes and gives mixtures (Section 10.2); it doesn't replace an OH group.

explanation: Primary and secondary alcohols are best converted into alkyl halides by treatment with either thionyl chloride (SOCl2) or phosphorus tribromide (PBr3). For example, 2-butanol and PBr3 in ether give 2-bromobutane (86%) and H3PO3.

prompt: Why are SOCl2 and PBr3 preferred over HX for primary and secondary alcohols?

choices.text: They are milder and less likely to cause acid-catalyzed rearrangements
They work only on tertiary alcohols, which react fastest
choices.why: SOCl2 and PBr3 are the reagents recommended for primary and secondary alcohols.

choices.text: They are more acidic than HX, so the reactions go faster
choices.why: They are less acidic than the HX method, and that is part of their advantage.

choices.text: They also convert ethers and carbonyl groups into alkyl halides
choices.why: Other functional groups such as ethers, carbonyls and aromatic rings usually don't interfere with these reactions.

explanation: The SOCl2 and PBr3 reactions normally take place readily under mild conditions, are less acidic and less likely to cause acid-catalyzed rearrangements than the HX method, give generally high yields, and usually aren't disturbed by ethers, carbonyls or aromatic rings.

prompt: According to the section, what is the most generally useful method for preparing alkyl halides?

choices.why: That gives mixtures of products, so it is a poor synthetic method (Section 10.2).

choices.text: Allylic bromination of alkenes with NBS
choices.why: NBS brominates only allylic positions, next to a double bond, so it isn't a general method.
Br2 addition gives only 1,2-dibromides. Alcohols are the most general starting materials.

explanation: The most generally useful method for preparing alkyl halides is to make them from alcohols, which themselves can be obtained from carbonyl compounds. Because of the importance of this process, many different methods have been developed to carry it out.

prompt: Which reagent from the section converts an alcohol into an alkyl fluoride?

choices.why: PBr3 converts primary and secondary alcohols into alkyl bromides.
SOCl2 converts alcohols into alkyl chlorides.
HCl converts tertiary alcohols into alkyl chlorides.

explanation: Alkyl fluorides can also be prepared from alcohols. Reagents include HF in pyridine solvent and diethylaminosulfur trifluoride, (CH3CH2)2NSF3. Cyclohexanol and HF in pyridine give fluorocyclohexane in 99% yield.

prompt: How would you prepare 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CCl, from an alcohol?

choices.why: 2-Methylpropane is an alkane with no OH group to replace. The starting material should be the alcohol, 2-methyl-2-propanol.
PBr3 makes alkyl bromides, not chlorides.
HF in pyridine makes alkyl fluorides, not chlorides.

explanation: 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane is a tertiary chloride. Its alcohol, 2-methyl-2-propanol, (CH3)3COH, is tertiary and reacts readily with HCl (Exercise 10.5.1a).

prompt: What is the best way to prepare 2-bromo-4-methylpentane, CH3CHBrCH2CH(CH3)2, from an alcohol?

choices.why: SOCl2 makes alkyl chlorides; PBr3 is the reagent for bromides.
The OH must be on the carbon that will carry the Br. This alcohol would give 1-bromo-4-methylpentane.
HF in pyridine makes alkyl fluorides, not bromides.

explanation: 2-Bromo-4-methylpentane is a secondary bromide. Secondary alcohols are best converted with PBr3, so treat 4-methyl-2-pentanol with PBr3 (Exercise 10.5.1b).

prompt: Which alcohol and reagent would you use to prepare 3-fluoro-1,1-dimethylcyclopentane?

choices.why: That alcohol has its OH next to the dimethyl carbon, so it would give 2-fluoro-1,1-dimethylcyclopentane.
PBr3 makes alkyl bromides, not fluorides.
HCl makes alkyl chlorides, not fluorides.

explanation: Fluorine replaces the OH group, so the alcohol must have its OH where the F will be, two carbons around the ring from the dimethyl carbon: 3,3-dimethylcyclopentanol. Alkyl fluorides are made from alcohols with HF in pyridine (Exercise 10.5.1d).
